vignette:
She still remembers the precise sound the sky made before it tore open. The typhoon arrived on a Tuesday afternoon in November, five years ago, when she was forty-seven. Her husband was at the hardware store, trying to buy sandbags that had already sold out. She was home alone, checking the weather alerts on her phone, when the wind shifted from a steady howl to a deep, grinding roar—like a freight train passing through her chest. The windows began to rattle in their frames, and then one of them shattered inward, spraying glass across the living room floor. She ran to the bathroom, the designated safe room, but the door wouldn’t lock. She pressed her back against the wall, clutching a towel to her face, and listened to the roof peel away in sections. For six hours, she stayed there, the roar never letting up, her legs shaking so badly she couldn’t stand. When the storm finally passed, she stepped out to find half her house gone—walls collapsed, furniture scattered in the neighbor’s yard, photographs turned to pulp in the mud. Her husband found her two hours later, standing ankle-deep in brown water, still holding the towel.

In the months after, she did what she had always done: she organized. She cleaned what she could, catalogued the losses, and threw herself into the rebuild. She returned to work at the public library within three weeks, partly because she needed the routine, partly because the library was one of the few buildings in town that had survived intact. The quiet there felt fortifying. She could shelve books, smile at patrons, and pretend the world was ordered again. But the quiet began to change on her. Now, when a patron slams a heavy reference book shut, she flinches. When the air conditioner hums too loudly, she feels sweat break out on her upper lip. On rainy days, she calls in sick—she cannot stand the sound of water hitting glass, cannot sit at her desk and listen to the drip-drip from a leaky window in the periodicals room. She tells her supervisor it’s a migraine. Her supervisor believes her, because she is reliable, and she has never lied before.

At home, she has rearranged the furniture three times. The couch must not face the windows. The television must be placed where she can see all doorways. She checks the weather app obsessively—sometimes twenty times an hour during monsoon season—and if the forecast shows more than a thirty percent chance of rain, she cannot sleep. Her husband tries to soothe her. He reminds her that the new roof is certified for category-five winds, that they have an emergency kit in the closet, that she is safe. She nods, says she knows, and then she spends the night on the floor of the bathroom, back against the wall, a towel in her hands. She has stopped telling him about it. He looks too tired when she does.

Her mind has become a room she cannot tidy. Images intrude without warning: the glass exploding, the ceiling collapsing, the muddy water rising over her sandals. She sees the face of her neighbor’s child, missing for two days before rescue workers found her alive. She hears the screams from the evacuation center, smells the damp concrete and rotting wood. When these memories come, her heart pounds so fast she thinks she might die, and she digs her fingernails into her palms until the pain pulls her back. She avoids the news. She declines invitations to community gatherings. She has stopped grocery shopping at the store near the coast because the parking lot flood drains remind her of the waterline marks on her walls.

At work, she still helps children find books about dinosaurs and helps elderly patrons navigate the computer catalog. She is polite, efficient, and admired. But she no lingers in the staff break room, no longer volunteers for evening story time. She arrives five minutes early, keeps her head down, and leaves exactly at closing time, umbrella always in her bag, even when the sky is clear. She tells herself she is fine. She is a librarian. She knows how to classify things, how to put disorder back in order. But the disorder inside her does not fit on any shelf.
